title: Ya-Sin, whole
hookLine: the messengers, the man who ran, the signs, the return (Surah 36)
tomorrow: what question does one surah ask again and again?

cards: When someone bursts into a room out of breath, every head turns. In Ya-Sin, a town has turned away the messengers sent to it and threatened them with stoning.

Then, in Pickthall's words: "And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent!" He isn't one of the messengers. He's one of the townspeople.
Why run? The answer hides in a strange gap a few lines later.

teach.b: He speaks his piece: why shouldn't I serve the One who made me, and to whom you'll all return? Then the surah cuts. No scene of what his people did to him.
The next line is simply: it was said, enter the Garden. Commentators fill the silence; the text leaves it. And his very first words there?
Would that my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me. Not revenge. Not relief.
He still wants good for the people who turned on him. That's the puzzle's answer: he ran because they were his. From there Ya-Sin turns to signs.
Dead earth brought to life. Night stripped from day.

teach.h: SUN, MOON, EACH IN AN ORBIT.
teach.b: "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit." Then the return.
A man picks up an old, crumbled bone and asks who could revive bones like this.
The answer: the One who made them the first time. And the line: "But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is."
Here's something to tell a friend, with its honest label: a report in Tirmidhi calls Ya-Sin the heart of the Qur'an, and scholars grade that report weak.
What the surah itself shows is enough: a man who cared about his people past the end, and a word that begins things again.

how: Some Muslims recite Ya-Sin for the dying and for those who have died, and at gatherings after a death, following reports that scholars grade differently; others read it at any time.

o: the name of the man who ran across the city
an Arabic word meaning the human heart
surah 36, opened by the two letters ya and sin

games.q: what happens in Ya-Sin — tap the pairs.
p: came from the far end of the city
his first words in the Garden
revived by the One who made it

s: the man who ran was one of the messengers
he was a townsman who came from the far end of the city to urge his people to follow them.
his first words in the Garden are about his own people
would that my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me (36:26–27).
it's firmly established that the Prophet called Ya-Sin the heart of the Qur'an
a report in Tirmidhi says so, and scholars grade that report weak.

games.q: your little cousin asks why the man in Ya-Sin ran across the city. the best answer from the surah?
o: he was running away from the town because he was scared.
to tell his own people to follow the messengers, out of care for them.
he was a messenger who arrived late and had to hurry.
games.why: he came running to his own people, and even in the Garden his first wish is that they knew. he ran because they were his.

practice: For the sit, listen to one sound: a recitation if you have one ready, or your own breathing if you don't. If there's someone you've lost, let them be near while you listen.
Some Muslims read Ya-Sin for those who have died; anyone can simply remember.

wordCard.voice: Ya-Sin. Two Arabic letters that open surah 36: the messengers, the man who ran, the signs, and the return.

orig.note: Arabic: be, and it is. the close of 36:82.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: be, and it is, the word that made things first and can make them again. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent!
